title: Forbidden Words
statement:
A moderation system has a list of `k` forbidden words (the same word may be listed more than once, and every listed word is counted separately). Given a message, count the **total number of occurrences** of all listed words in it, where an occurrence is a position at which the word appears as a substring, and **overlapping occurrences all count**. For example the words `a`, `aa` and `aaa` occur `4 + 3 + 2 = 9` times in `aaaa`.

**Input.** The first line holds `k`. The next `k` lines hold one word each. The last line holds the message. All strings consist of lowercase letters `a` to `z`.

**Output.** The total number of occurrences.
constraints: 1 ≤ k; the total length of all words is at most 20000 in this browser version (the idea scales to 10^6)
The answer can exceed 32 bits in larger inputs: use 64-bit integers

hints: Searching each word separately with KMP costs O(k * message length) in total, too slow when there are thousands of words. Can the words share the work?

Put all words in one trie. Reading the message letter by letter, keep the longest suffix of what you have read that is a prefix of some word: that is a trie node. When the next letter has no child, you must fall back to a shorter suffix, which is what a failure link stores.

Build failure links with a breadth-first search over the trie, and complete the missing transitions so that every state has a move for every letter. Let cnt[state] be the number of words that are suffixes of the state's string: cnt[state] = words ending exactly there + cnt[fail[state]]. Add cnt of the current state after every letter.
editorial: Build an **Aho-Corasick automaton**. First insert all words into a trie; `cnt[v]` counts the words ending exactly at node `v`. Define the **failure link** `fail[v]` of a node as the node for the longest proper suffix of `v`'s string that is also a prefix of some word (it is the KMP prefix function lifted to a trie). Process the nodes in breadth-first order so that shallower nodes are finished first: for a node `u` and a letter `c` with child `v`, set `fail[v] = go[fail[u]][c]` and push `v`; if `u` has no child for `c`, store `go[u][c] = go[fail[u]][c]` so that the transition table is complete and scanning never has to follow failure links one by one. Because every word that is a suffix of `v`'s string also ends at `v`, accumulate `cnt[u] += cnt[fail[u]]` in the same breadth-first order (the failure target is shallower, hence already final). Scanning the message is then one table lookup per letter, adding `cnt[state]` each time, which counts every occurrence of every word, overlaps included, and handles repeated words because each listed copy increments `cnt`. Building costs `O(total length * 26)` with a dense table, scanning costs `O(message length)`. The answer can be large (many words ending at every position), so use 64-bit counters in languages with fixed-width integers.

import sys

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
k = int(data[0])
patterns = data[1:1 + k]
text = data[1 + k]

go = [[-1] * 26]                       # go[state][letter]
cnt = [0]                              # how many patterns end exactly at this state
for p in patterns:                     # build the trie
    s = 0
    for ch in p:
        c = ord(ch) - 97
        if go[s][c] == -1:
            go.append([-1] * 26)
            cnt.append(0)
            go[s][c] = len(go) - 1
        s = go[s][c]
    cnt[s] += 1
fail = [0] * len(go)
queue = []
for c in range(26):
    v = go[0][c]
    if v == -1:
        go[0][c] = 0
    else:
        queue.append(v)
for u in queue:                        # breadth first: shallower states are finished first
    cnt[u] += cnt[fail[u]]             # patterns that are suffixes of this state's string also end here
    for c in range(26):
        v = go[u][c]
        if v == -1:
            go[u][c] = go[fail[u]][c]  # complete the automaton: follow the failure link instead
        else:
            fail[v] = go[fail[u]][c]
            queue.append(v)
state, total = 0, 0
for ch in text:
    state = go[state][ord(ch) - 97]
    total += cnt[state]
print(total)
